classification.tone: Propulsive, paranoid, witty, and emotionally bruised

evaluation.positioning_hook: A disgraced tech prodigy starts receiving capsules from his future self, only to learn his comeback is built on a murder conspiracy that can erase people from time.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and commercially legible: a fallen inventor, a future-self message engine, and a conspiracy that turns every choice into a survival move. The script also gives the audience a strong emotional spine through Elliot and Robyn, which broadens it beyond pure concept.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately with Park’s opening murder-suicide, Elliot’s capsule discovery, and the rule that future messages arrive as actionable instructions. The story engine is easy to explain in one breath, and the stakes sharpen cleanly once Wilkes is revealed as the architect.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Elliot is a strong lead because his self-loathing, intelligence, and dry humor all play in the same role, and Robyn gives the story a grounded counterweight with real emotional authority. Craig, Prescott, and Wilkes each have distinct energy, though the movie is still primarily powered by the central trio.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar time-travel idea and makes it feel like a corporate assassination thriller with memory as the tracking mechanism. The choice to make the future self both mentor and manipulator gives the material a sharper edge than a standard sci-fi chase.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps escalating through clear reversals: the museum hit, the lottery bait, the hitman trap, the Craig betrayal, and the Wilkes reveal. Each new capsule changes the game, and the final lab siege pays off the engine with real forward drive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of time travel as a weaponized corporate moat feels fresh and immediately usable, especially with the memory-tracking rule and the self-authored future conceit. It’s novel in a way that still clicks fast, which is the sweet spot for this kind of material.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The tech-world setting has real texture: basements, demos, venture-style status games, private security, and the prestige of Silicon Valley success. The world is not sprawling, but it is specific enough to generate story and to make the power dynamics feel lived-in.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct blend of sardonic banter, noir paranoia, and high-concept sci-fi dread. Elliot’s self-deprecating jokes sit right next to gunplay, surgery, and existential dread, which gives the movie a recognizable voice.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the thriller mechanics, the script is really about self-authorship, regret, addiction, and whether intelligence without self-belief can ever become wisdom. The Robyn/Elliot material especially suggests a deeper emotional movie beneath the chase.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Elliot/Robyn is the strongest relationship engine, and Craig/Wilkes/Prescott all create useful pressure points around him. The ensemble is functional and often lively, though the movie still lives most strongly in the central pair and the triangle of male rivals.

notable_requirements: San Francisco and Los Angeles settings
Tech campus, mansion, motel, storage unit, post office, museum, and lab environments

technical.vfx_details: Capsule holograms, time-materialization effects, disintegration effects, and a few stylized transition moments; mostly contained and repeatable.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, car impacts, fireball/lab destruction, practical blood effects, and a car-over-hill sequence.

rights_flags.detail: LACMA, Altria, Aston Martin, Hugo Boss, Manolo, iPad-like device, Stack/StackPhone/StackPad references, Rohypnol, Dexedrine, Klonopin, Zoloft, Ambien, Xanax, Fats Domino, Jason Mraz, Road House
Kierkegaard and President Obama are referenced by name.
The script uses a named song cue, 'Blueberry Hill,' and multiple recognizable brand and product references.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Premium streaming or theatrical genre lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release with strong festival-to-platform or mid-budget theatrical potential; the engine is a contained sci-fi thriller with escalating reveals.

cost.note: Contemporary settings keep the footprint manageable, but the lab fire, car action, multiple city locations, and hologram effects push it above a lean indie.

cast.note: The story can be built around a few strong leads, but it benefits from specific casting in the Elliot, Robyn, Wilkes, Craig, and Prescott roles.

location.note: The script moves through San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Thailand, with several distinct interiors that each carry story weight.

content.note: Gun violence, suicide, drugging, torture-adjacent coercion, and a lab inferno place this firmly in mature territory.

rights.note: The script names multiple brands, real-world venues, and a specific song cue, all of which would need clearance review.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The premise turns memory into a tracking device.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the movie a clean, cinematic rule set and a fresh way to stage paranoia without relying on generic surveillance tech. Buyers who want a high-concept thriller with a built-in engine will see a hook that is easy to market and easy to cut a trailer around.
strengths.evidence: Elliot realizes the capsules can be tracked through what he remembers, and Robyn helps him travel blind to break the chain.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Elliot is built for a star turn.
strengths.what_it_means: The role gives an actor intelligence, self-loathing, comic timing, and physical jeopardy in the same package, which is exactly the kind of part that can reframe a career. Mid-career leads looking for a prestige genre showcase will chase this, and managers can sell it as a rare chance to play wounded, funny, and dangerous at once.
strengths.evidence: He goes from hungover basement coder to swaggering comeback figure to terrified man in a garage, all while keeping the same dry voice.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Robyn gives the movie its emotional ballast.
strengths.what_it_means: She is not just the love interest; she becomes the audience’s translator, co-strategist, and moral witness, which makes the central relationship feel like a real engine rather than a decorative one. Actors who want a sharp, capable female lead with intimacy, skepticism, and nerve will respond to her immediately.
strengths.evidence: She doses Elliot to keep him safe, helps decode the capsules, performs the improvised surgery, and forces the truth into the open.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The villain is a corporate futurist with a god complex.
strengths.what_it_means: Wilkes is not a generic madman; he is a polished, persuasive founder whose charisma makes the threat feel plausible and contemporary. That opens the door for a magnetic supporting performance and gives the project a buyer-friendly antagonist who can sell both prestige and genre.
strengths.evidence: His DigiCon speech, his private lab, and his calm explanation of using time to protect intellectual property all frame him as a tech-world predator.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script keeps escalating with new capsule reveals.
strengths.what_it_means: Each message changes the rules of the game, so the movie never settles into a single-note chase; it keeps retooling itself into a bigger thriller. That kind of escalation is valuable for producers because it creates a trailer-friendly structure and a strong act-to-act momentum curve.
strengths.evidence: The story moves from lottery numbers to self-improvement to hit-man instructions to the final reveal of Wilkes’ future lab.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tech-world setting has real status texture.
strengths.what_it_means: This is not a generic lab movie; it lives in the language of demos, funding, product launches, and prestige competition, which makes the stakes feel current and exportable. It will appeal to buyers who want a contemporary thriller with Silicon Valley energy rather than a purely abstract sci-fi premise.
strengths.evidence: Altria, Trinity, DigiCon, venture-style rivalries, and the public humiliation of Radius all give the world a recognizable corporate ecosystem.

whats_special.headline: This is a smart, commercial sci-fi thriller with a clean hook, a wounded lead role actors will chase, and a villain whose power comes from the modern tech economy. It has the rare combination of high-concept clarity, emotional access, and contained enough production design to feel achievable without losing scale.

lead_characters.name: Elliot Lockhart / Radius
lead_characters.hook: A brilliant, self-sabotaging engineer with a razor-dry mouth and a collapsing self-image, Elliot is the kind of man who can talk himself into and out of greatness in the same breath. He’s funny when he’s cornered, wounded when he’s performing confidence, and always one bad decision away from disaster, which makes him compelling even before the time-travel engine kicks in.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Keaton in Birdman crossed with Jake Gyllenhaal in Nightcrawler: a lead who can weaponize charm while revealing panic underneath it. It gives an actor the full range of comeback narrative, dark comedy, and physical survival, the kind of role that can redefine how the industry sees him.

lead_characters.name: Robyn Gilmore
lead_characters.hook: Robyn is sharp, skeptical, and emotionally literate, with enough medical competence and nerve to keep the story from floating away into pure concept. She has the rare quality of being both the person who sees through Elliot and the person who still chooses to stand beside him, which gives her real dramatic authority.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Emily Blunt in Sicario or Rebecca Ferguson in Mission: Impossible — a woman who can carry intelligence, tension, and emotional restraint without ever feeling ornamental. It gives an actress a role that is active, grounded, and essential to the plot, with enough intimacy to play as a true co-lead.

lead_characters.name: Jonathan Wilkes
lead_characters.hook: Wilkes is a polished tech visionary with the smile of a founder and the instincts of a warlord, which makes him dangerous in a very modern way. He speaks like a man who believes history belongs to the people who can author it, and that confidence gives him real menace.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad or Michael Shannon in Take Shelter: a charismatic intelligence that can turn predatory without changing volume. It gives an actor the chance to play seduction, authority, and moral rot in one role, which is catnip for prestige casting.

lead_characters.name: Craig Bollinger
lead_characters.hook: Craig is the swaggering best friend who looks like he’s winning at life until the script reveals how much of that confidence is performance. He’s funny, socially fluent, and deeply compromised, which makes him feel like a real Silicon Valley survivor rather than a stock sidekick.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jonah Hill in The Wolf of Wall Street or Jeremy Strong in Succession — a fast-talking operator whose charm curdles into betrayal. It gives an actor a juicy pivot from comic ally to tragic pressure point, which is exactly the kind of role that gets noticed.

lead_characters.name: David Prescott
lead_characters.hook: Prescott is the younger boss who enjoys being the guy with the clipboard, but the script keeps letting us see the insecurity under the smugness. He’s petty, ambitious, and ultimately trapped in the same future-pressure system as everyone else, which makes him more than a simple office antagonist.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Paul Dano in There Will Be Blood or Matthew Macfadyen in Succession — a tightly wound man whose authority is always one crack away from humiliation. It gives an actor a role built on brittle control, resentment, and sudden panic.

lead_characters.name: Harold
lead_characters.hook: Harold is the quiet institutional ghost of the building, the one person who understands the machinery of the place better than the executives do. He has warmth, discretion, and a lived-in dignity that makes him feel like the moral memory of the company.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Richard Jenkins in The Visitor — a small role with real humanity and authority. Character actors will chase it because it gives them a scene-stealing presence without needing volume.

lead_characters.name: Meredith Rothert
lead_characters.hook: Meredith is introduced as a stylish, self-possessed young woman whose presence in the museum sequence is loaded with mystery before the script reveals her place in the larger machine. Even in limited screen time, she carries the eerie sense of a life already being written by someone else.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that plays like the haunting, compressed showcase of Alicia Vikander in Ex Machina — brief, elegant, and loaded with implication. It gives an actress a memorable entry point in a high-concept thriller with a strong visual imprint.

lead_characters.name: Franklin Gantt
lead_characters.hook: Gantt is the polished corporate patriarch who can smell opportunity and danger in the same room. He reads as a man who has survived long enough to know when to pivot, which makes him a useful power broker in the story’s ecosystem.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of John Lithgow in a prestige corporate drama — a senior executive role with intelligence, vanity, and leverage. It gives an actor a chance to play the man who can bless or bury the future with a handshake.

lead_characters.name: Maguire
lead_characters.hook: Maguire is the professional killer who never raises his voice unless he has to, which makes him feel scarier than a louder villain. He has a working-man’s bluntness and a dead-eyed discipline that turns every scene into a negotiation with death.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom — a calm, predatory presence whose menace comes from understatement. It gives an actor a lean, memorable antagonist role with real scene-control.

lead_characters.name: Lola
lead_characters.hook: Lola is the social spark who turns Elliot’s humiliation into a public event, but she’s not just a device; she has the kind of bright, status-aware energy that makes the tech-party world feel real. She’s playful, curious, and a little ruthless in the way she reads people.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Olivia Wilde in a sharp social satire — a brief role with instant charisma and bite. It gives an actress a memorable scene in a movie where social humiliation matters as much as gunfire.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a paranoid sci-fi thriller with emotional bruises under the machinery.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie or prestige-leaning genre directors with at least one or two features, especially those who like performance-forward tension, clean visual rules, and morally compromised protagonists. The material rewards directors who can balance sleek tech-world surfaces with intimate dread and make exposition feel like pressure rather than explanation.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a contained but escalating canvas: offices, labs, hotels, and a few big set pieces, all driven by character choices rather than spectacle for its own sake. It’s the kind of project that attracts filmmakers who want to prove they can do high-concept genre without losing adult emotion.

buyer_appeal.lane: Premium streamer / mid-budget theatrical sci-fi thriller lane
buyer_appeal.detail: It can be built around a small number of strong roles and a contemporary footprint, so it does not require a giant ensemble or tentpole-scale effects to work. The time-travel premise, tech-world setting, and clear trailer hook give it export value and a clean pitch for buyers looking for elevated genre with adult appeal.

considerations.area: The middle can keep tightening around the capsule rules.
considerations.detail: The script is strongest when each capsule changes the game, and the version of the middle where every new message either raises the stakes or reveals a new layer of the conspiracy would keep the momentum razor-sharp. One primary lever would be to make sure the Robyn/Elliot decoding scenes always arrive with a fresh turn, so the audience feels the engine advancing rather than repeating.

considerations.area: The supporting world can stay leaner without losing texture.
considerations.detail: The story already has enough moving parts in Elliot, Robyn, Wilkes, Craig, Prescott, and Maguire, so any future pass could consider folding or trimming peripheral beats that don’t change the power map. That would protect the pace and keep the movie centered on the relationships that actually drive the thriller.

considerations.area: The opening museum sequence does a lot of setup work.
considerations.detail: The Park/Meredith prologue is a strong cold open, and it also carries a lot of rule-setting before the movie fully shifts to Elliot. A next pass could explore whether one or two of the explanatory beats there can be delivered through image or later payoff, so the opening lands even faster.

considerations.area: The brand and music references will need a clearance pass.
considerations.detail: The script names multiple consumer brands, real venues, and a specific song cue, which is normal for a contemporary tech-world piece but does require a practical review. If a producer wants the cleanest path, the version of the script where a few of those references are generalized would preserve the movie’s feel while simplifying paperwork.

considerations.area: The final lab siege is the biggest production swing.
considerations.detail: The fire, the capsule effects, the security-team action, and the lab destruction all stack into the movie’s most expensive sequence. The story earns it, but a producer could also consider how much of that climax can be staged through contained practical effects and selective VFX to protect the budget without shrinking the payoff.
